objections.claim: The writer's completeness check exists to make it impossible for a criterion to "disappear without a trace" — the spec's own anti-pattern is "letting the evaluator emit `delegated[]` and having the writer trust it." But in the inline path, `faff holdout record --spec <path>` is invoked by `holdout_step` running **in the judged party's own lane** (top-level/sequential graft runs it in-lane). The agent chooses which file `--spec` names. Nothing pins that file to the text the evaluator actually judged: no hash, no cached classify output, no binding to the evaluate step. An agent that wants a criterion omitted writes a trimmed spec copy (drop the scenario, or reword the DONE item to prose), passes that path, and the writer's classify run then derives a judged set that matches the trimmed block. The record validates clean, `delegated[]` is derived from the doctored spec, and the merge floor sees a self-consistent `meets-spec`. The control the ticket introduces is rekeyed by the adversary it exists against — the same fail-open the spec rejects one level down ("the writer, not the LLM"), relocated to the flag that feeds the writer.

objections.claim: The spec presents two follow-ups that "narrow" the trust shift for delegated prose DONE items: FAFF-1339 and moving the checklist write to the trusted side. FAFF-1339 checks that a `delegated[].ac_id` with verifier `ac-checklist` has a `passed:true` row in the same anchor — but both the `delegated[]` listing and `ac-checklist.json` (including its `passed` flags) are builder-authored in-lane artifacts. The check verifies internal consistency of one lane's own attestations; it adds no independence and therefore does not narrow the trust shift at all. Only the trusted-side write does.
objections.evidence: Spec §3, "The trust shift for prose DONE items" ("Two follow-ups narrow it: FAFF-1339 … and moving the checklist write to the trusted side") and the Out-of-scope FAFF-1339 bullet ("makes the merge floor fail when a `delegated[].ac_id` … has no `passed:true` row in the same anchor"). The spec itself concedes the checklist is builder-authored rung-0 and "Neither is independent of the lane."

objections.claim: Listing `integration` rows in `delegated[]` makes the FAFF-961 handoff durable and visible, but the verifier recorded for those rows (`review-merge-floor`) cannot act on ids — the spec's own delegation-scope argument establishes that nothing receives a Scenarios unit by id, and the review floor reads the spec, not the record. So the "trace" for integration rows is a passive label on what remains a prompt-only handoff, and unlike the `ac-checklist` verifier (which gets FAFF-1339), no follow-up is filed or named for `review-merge-floor` rows. The claim that this "closes FAFF-961's gap" is true only for visibility, not for enforcement, and the spec does not say which.

objections.claim: Before this change, a prose DONE item forced the holdout aggregate to `needs-human`, and the strict L4 floor blocked — an independent, code-blind verifier stood between the item and the merge. After this change, the same item is verified only by `ac-checklist.json`, which the builder writes in-lane (the rung-0 posture the spec itself restates), attesting `all_verified` and per-criterion `passed` over its own work. At ship time there is no mechanical check that a `delegated[].ac_id` has any checklist row at all (FAFF-1339 is out of scope), and the trusted-side checklist write is also out of scope. The only independent compensating control is the review leg, which sees the checklist but does not re-execute it. The net effect is that the actor being judged becomes the sole attester for every delegated criterion, and the spec ships that state rather than sequencing a hardening follow-up into it.
objections.evidence: "The trust shift for prose DONE items" — "a prose item now rests on the builder's own attestation plus the review leg… Neither is independent of the lane in the way the old block was"; Out of scope defers both FAFF-1339 and the trusted-side checklist write; ac-29 only requires the docs to *say* this.
objections.predicted_consequence: A builder whose prose DONE items are unmet ticks them in its own `ac-checklist.json` (or omits rows entirely, undetected until FAFF-1339), the holdout records `meets-spec` over the judged set, and the merge floor passes on the builder's self-attestation alone.
objections.disposition_rationale: Product owner accepted the trust shift on 2026-10-17: delegated prose rests on the builder-written AC checklist plus the review leg, stated in the spec; FAFF-1339 and a trusted-side checklist write are the follow-ups.

objections.claim: The design inverts the incentive on classification. Previously, phrasing a requirement as prose DONE *punished* the spec (hard `needs-human` block); after this change it *rewards* it — the item leaves code-blind judgement and lands on the builder-controlled checklist leg. This is adversarially exploitable because the tier rule is shape-based and the spec author controls the shape: any criterion — including a security-relevant one — can be written as a prose DONE item to route it to `delegated`/`ac-checklist`. The spec's own precedence rule makes this stronger: a DONE prose item containing "rollback" is explicitly tiered `delegated` *ahead of* the integration-keyword check, so an author can phrase a rollback/reversal requirement as prose and move it off the review/merge test floor (which runs the build's own tests) onto the builder's self-attestation. The spec's mis-tiering analysis considers only *accidental* mis-tiering ("authors who want code-blind coverage phrase the item with Then or must") and adds no heuristic; its only structural answer, FAFF-1293, covers prose *Scenarios* units, not prose DONE items, which remain legal and now advantageous.
objections.evidence: "Which prose criteria are delegated" PROCEDURE step 2 (prose+done → delegated before the keyword check); "Prose DONE with an integration keyword? Chosen: tier it delegated"; "Mis-tiering. Chosen: no new mis-tier heuristic in this slice"; Out of scope excludes any gating check in `faff admissible`.
objections.predicted_consequence: A spec whose substantive requirements are systematically phrased as prose DONE items produces `judged_count` near zero, a trivially satisfiable holdout, and a merge resting entirely on the builder's own checklist — with the non-gating advisory as the only signal.
objections.disposition_rationale: Product owner accepted the trust shift on 2026-10-17: delegated prose rests on the builder-written AC checklist plus the review leg, stated in the spec; FAFF-1339 and a trusted-side checklist write are the follow-ups. A non-gating advisory now flags a spec whose DONE items are all prose with nothing judged.

objections.claim: `cmdHoldoutRecord` takes the evaluator block on stdin (`fs.readFileSync(0)`), and the spec defines `--spec <path|->`. If `-` means stdin for the spec, both the block and the classify input are drawn from the same stream with no defined framing — the second read gets whatever the first left (typically empty, yielding a spurious "unreadable spec" refusal) or, worse, a caller that concatenates the two documents gets one of them silently mis-parsed. The failure path here is fail-closed (exit 2 / refusal), so this is a hardening edit, not a bypass — but the spec should either drop `-` or define the framing.
objections.evidence: "cmdHoldoutRecord gains a required --spec <path|->"; context `cmdHoldoutRecord` reads the block via `fs.readFileSync(0, "utf8")`.
objections.predicted_consequence: An inline invocation using `--spec -` writes no record or writes a fail-closed record derived from a mis-framed spec; the operator gets an confusing refusal rather than a defined error.

objections.claim: The new validator rules (reject `done:N` prose, duplicate-id, completeness matching) all depend on `criteria[].id` being present in the raw block that `computeHoldoutVerdict` receives — but `holdout-verdict.schema.json`'s `criteria` items are `additionalProperties: false` with only `class`, `verdict`, `evidence_present` in `properties`. The spec asserts "the id rules need no change to the criteria items of `holdout-verdict.schema.json`" and justifies it by citing `holdout-anchored.schema.json` (the *record* schema), not the contract schema the block is shaped by. The spec never states whether the contract path schema-validates the input block, and never says whether `id` is added to the contract schema (which, note, *would* be additive: optional, closed, `additionalProperties` is false).
objections.evidence: "### Validator rules" — "The raw block already carries `criteria[].id` (required by `holdout-anchored.schema.json`)"; ac-10, ac-12, ac-14.
objections.predicted_consequence: A build can satisfy ac-10/ac-12/ac-14 (compute-fn violations fire on ids) while the reference contract schema rejects every conformant block for carrying `id` — or, on a build that adds `id` to the schema, ac-6's "byte-identical copies" scope silently expands. The tester cannot tell which of the two the spec intends.

objections.claim: ac-27 requires a test that re-classifies "the committed specs of the four anchors that carry `holdout.json`" and matches them against "every criterion the committed record judged as `scenario` or `assertion`". Two things are unstated: (1) where the committed specs live and whether all four are retrievable in-repo; (2) the matching key. FAFF-1259's ids are recent — if any of the four committed records is legacy (the spec itself says "Legacy records without ids … validate as before"), its criteria rows carry no `id`, and the record also does not carry `source`, so "only `done`-sourced prose moved to `delegated`" cannot be decided from the record at all: a prose row with no id cannot be attributed to `done` vs `scenarios` except by fuzzy text matching, which the spec does not define.
